title: Erdős Problem #1008: C₄-Free Subgraphs
description: Does every graph with m edges contain a C₄-free subgraph with ≫ m^{2/3} edges? Yes, proved by Conlon-Fox-Sudakov (2014). The exponent 2/3 is optimal, as shown by Folkman's counterexample K_{n,n²}.

meta.author: Conlon-Fox-Sudakov (2014)
meta.assumptions: 1 axiom: Conlon-Fox-Sudakov main theorem (Ω(m^{2/3}) C₄-free subgraph). Proved: Kővári-Sós-Turán C₄-case (cherry counting+CS), K₂₂↔C₄ equivalence, C₄-freeness hereditary/monotone, common neighbor uniqueness, few-edges C₄-free, Folkman ratio, bipartite KST (cherry counting on K_{n,n²}), exponent 2/3 optimality.

overview.historicalContext: This problem was originally posed by Bollobás and Erdős at the 1966 Tihany graph theory colloquium in Hungary, asking whether every m-edge graph contains a C₄-free subgraph with ≫ m^{3/4} edges. Folkman quickly disproved this using the bipartite graph K_{n,n²}: it has n³ edges but every C₄-free subgraph has only O(n²) = O(m^{2/3}) edges, by the Kővári-Sós-Turán theorem. Erdős revised the conjecture to exponent 2/3 in 1971, noting that the trivial bound m^{1/2} follows easily from Kővári-Sós-Turán. He mentioned that Szemerédi had proved the 2/3 bound but gave no published reference. The problem remained formally open until Conlon, Fox, and Sudakov proved it in their 2014 paper using dependent random choice, a powerful probabilistic technique developed in the 2000s. A simpler proof was later given by Hunter. The result fits into the broader program of understanding Turán-type and Zarankiewicz-type problems: how dense can a graph be while avoiding a fixed forbidden subgraph? The C₄ case is special because C₄ = K_{2,2}, linking cycle-free conditions to bipartite Ramsey theory.
overview.problemStatement: Does every graph with m edges contain a subgraph with ≫ m^{2/3} edges which contains no C₄ (4-cycle)?
overview.text: Does every graph with m edges contain a C₄-free subgraph with ≫ m^{2/3} edges? Yes, proved by Conlon-Fox-Sudakov (2014). The exponent 2/3 is optimal, as shown by Folkman's counterexample K_{n,n²}.
overview.proofStrategy: The formalization proves the Kővári-Sós-Turán theorem (C₄ case) via cherry counting and Cauchy-Schwarz, the K₂₂↔C₄ equivalence, structural properties (hereditary, monotone, common neighbor uniqueness, few-edges lemma), Folkman's ratio computation, and the exponent 2/3 optimality theorem. The one remaining axiom — Conlon-Fox-Sudakov main theorem — requires probabilistic method machinery not yet in Mathlib.
keyInsights: **C₄ = K_{2,2}:** The 4-cycle is the smallest complete bipartite graph, making C₄-freeness equivalent to K_{2,2}-freeness and connecting to the Zarankiewicz problem
**Folkman's Optimality Proof:** K_{n,n²} has m = n³ edges but only O(n²) = O(m^{2/3}) edges in any C₄-free subgraph, proving the exponent 2/3 cannot be improved
**Dependent Random Choice:** The Conlon-Fox-Sudakov proof selects a random vertex set S, takes common neighborhoods, and uses the probabilistic method to find a large C₄-free subgraph
**Zarankiewicz Generalization:** The result extends to K_{s,t}-free subgraphs with exponent 1-1/s, where the C₄ case is s=t=2

sections.title: 4-Cycles, C₄-Freeness, and K_{s,t}
sections.summary: HasC4 (4-cycle detection), IsC4Free, HasKst (complete bipartite subgraph) definitions
sections.mathContext: A 4-cycle $C_4$ in a graph $G$ is a sequence of distinct vertices $a, b, c, d$ with edges $ab, bc, cd, da$. Equivalently, $C_4 \cong K_{2,2}$: four vertices forming a complete bipartite subgraph with parts $\{a,c\}$ and $\{b,d\}$. A graph is $C_4$-free if it contains no such subgraph.

sections.title: K_{2,2} = C₄ Equivalence (Proved)
sections.summary: Full proof that K_{2,2} ↔ C₄ via Finset extraction and disjointness
sections.mathContext: The equivalence $K_{2,2} \cong C_4$ is the fundamental link between 4-cycle freeness and the Zarankiewicz problem. Forward: extract 2 vertices from each part of $K_{2,2}$ and verify the 4-cycle. Backward: given $a$-$b$-$c$-$d$-$a$, take $S = \{a,c\}$, $T = \{b,d\}$.

sections.title: Structural Properties (Proved)
sections.summary: C₄-freeness is hereditary, monotone; common neighbor uniqueness; few-edges lemma
sections.mathContext: Key structural results: (1) C₄-freeness passes to subgraphs. (2) In a $C_4$-free graph, any two vertices share at most one common neighbor (if two existed, they'd form a $C_4$). (3) A graph with $\le 3$ edges is always $C_4$-free since a $C_4$ needs exactly 4 distinct edges.

sections.title: Folkman's Counterexample (Proved)
sections.summary: Folkman ratio computation: (n³)^{2/3} = n², proving 2/3 is tight
sections.mathContext: The complete bipartite graph $K_{n,n^2}$ has $m = n^3$ edges. The Folkman ratio $m^{2/3}/m^{2/3} = n^2/n^2 = 1$ shows the exponent $2/3$ is best possible.

sections.title: Kővári-Sós-Turán Theorem (Proved)
sections.summary: Full proof of KST C₄ case via cherry counting + Cauchy-Schwarz: 4m² ≤ n²(n-1) + 2mn
sections.mathContext: The Kővári-Sós-Turán theorem for $C_4$-free graphs: if $G$ has $n$ vertices, $m$ edges, and is $C_4$-free, then $4m^2 \le n^2(n-1) + 2mn$, giving $m = O(n^{3/2})$. Proved via: (1) Cherry counting — offDiag neighborhoods are pairwise disjoint by $C_4$-freeness, giving $\sum d(v)(d(v)-1) \le n(n-1)$; (2) Cauchy-Schwarz — $(\sum d(v))^2 \le n \cdot \sum d(v)^2$; (3) Handshaking lemma — $\sum d(v) = 2m$.

sections.title: Main Theorems (Partially Axiomatized)
sections.summary: Bipartite KST helpers (KB, bip_cherry_disjoint/count, bip_edge_bound) + axiom erdos_1008 (CFS conjecture) + proved theorems: exponent_optimal (2/3 is tight) and c4free_subgraph_exists
sections.mathContext: One axiomatized result: **Erdős #1008** (Conlon-Fox-Sudakov 2014, line 590): $\exists c > 0$ such that every $m$-edge graph has a $C_4$-free subgraph with $\ge c \cdot m^{2/3}$ edges. Proved: Exponent optimality (line 605) — for every $\varepsilon > 0$, some graph has no $C_4$-free subgraph with $m^{2/3+\varepsilon}$ edges, via Folkman's $K_{n,n^2}$ construction and bipartite cherry counting. Existence (line 690) — every graph has such a subgraph.

conclusion.summary: Every graph with m edges contains a C₄-free subgraph with Ω(m^{2/3}) edges, proved by Conlon-Fox-Sudakov (2014) using dependent random choice. The exponent 2/3 is optimal, matching Folkman's upper bound from K_{n,n²}. The result generalizes to K_{s,t}-free subgraphs with exponent 1-1/s, connecting to the classical Zarankiewicz problem.
conclusion.implications:
**Theoretical Significance**: This result exemplifies the power of dependent random choice in extremal combinatorics. It shows that even dense graphs contain large sparse (forbidden-subgraph-free) subgraphs, with tight bounds.

The technique has applications in additive combinatorics, theoretical computer science (graph sparsification), and Ramsey theory. The Zarankiewicz-type generalization provides a unified framework for understanding how different forbidden subgraphs control the density of extractable subgraphs.
openQuestions: What are the optimal constants in the Ω(m^{2/3}) bound?
Can such subgraphs be found algorithmically in polynomial time?
What happens for odd cycle-freeness (C₅, C₇, ...) instead of C₄?
Can the K_{s,t} generalization be extended to non-bipartite forbidden graphs?
What is the weighted version: maximize edge-weight sum in a C₄-free subgraph?
